messages.subject: Re: AHM2's CAR models in NIMBLE (and in parallel)
messages.subject_clean: AHM2's CAR models in NIMBLE (and in parallel)
messages.body_plain:
Hello Mike,

have you found any solution to this?

Tomas

On Tue, 23 Mar 2021 at 09:03, Mike Meredith <stats...@gmail.com> wrote:

> The comment about runs "taking up to 5 days" refers to the original WinBUGS code (specifically the model in section 3.4.5). With the same number of iterations and chains in series, NIMBLE would take about 15 hours. With more, shorter chains run in parallel and with less (but still adequate) burn-in, the time could be reduced below 2hrs.
>
> NIMBLE is  much faster than WinBUGS for these models.
> On Tuesday, March 9, 2021 at 10:25:42 AM UTC+8 Mike Meredith wrote:
> >
> > Kéry & Royle (2021) Applied Hierarchical Modeling Vol.2 (AHM2) includes 5 spatial auto-regressive CAR models, 2 in chapter 3 and 3 in chapter 9. The code is available at the AHM_code GitHub repository <https://github.com/mikemeredith/AHM_code>.
> >
> > Since JAGS will not do spatial auto-correlation models, these were coded in good ol' WinBUGS 1.4. WinBUGS is specific to the Windows OS. It is no longer maintained, and is not guaranteed to work on future Windows upgrades. The relatively new NIMBLE package will do spatial models, and I have 'translated' the WinBUGS code to run with nimble::nimbleMCMC. See the files tagged "..._nimble.R" here and here.
> >
> > These models mix poorly and long runs are required, taking up to 5 days. It makes sense to run chains in parallel and to use as many cores as possible. Unlike jagsUI::jags, neither R2WinBUGS::bugs nor nimble::nimbleMCMC has built-in capability for parallel processing. Multiple instances can, however, be run in parallel using the CRAN package foreach. I've added code to implement this to the scripts in the AHM_code repository. See more information on using foreach here <https://mmeredith.net/blog/2021/parallel_chains_foreach.htm>.
> >
> > The model in section 9.5 caused problems. In WinBUGS, it often throws an error, "Undefined real result". Kéry & Royle advise retrying multiple times. With foreach, with the argument .errorhandling='remove', it's easy to discard chains that throw errors and recover the results of those that run properly.
> >
> > With this model, NIMBLE does not throw an error but prints a warning, "logProb is -Inf". It runs, but some of the random walk samplers are stuck at their starting values (with acceptance rate 0). The problem occurs when several of the starting values generated automatically by NIMBLE are far out in the tails of the posterior distribution, so that the probability of the model is effectively zero.
> >
> > I identified and discarded the "stuck" chains and looked at the posterior distributions of the top-level stochastic nodes from those that worked. Based on that information, I added values to the inits function, with random draws from uniform distributions somewhat wider than the CrIs of the posteriors. The model than ran properly. More details and diagnostic plots are here <https://mmeredith.net/blog/2021/starting_values_convergence.htm>.
> >

> --
> *** Three hierarchical modeling email lists ***
> (1) unmarked: for questions specific to the R package unmarked
> (2) SCR: for design and Bayesian or non-bayesian analysis of spatial capture-recapture
> (3) HMecology (this list): for everything else, especially material covered in the books by Royle & Dorazio (2008), Kéry & Schaub (2012), Kéry & Royle (2016, 2020)

> Dear all,

> Michael Schaub and I have written a textbook about integrated population models (IPMs), which Academic Press will publish later in 2021. The book will have 650 pages and two parts: in the first part, we describe the theory of IPMs in 10 chapters, while in the second part, we present 11 shorter chapters with case studies, and then there is also a short chapter with Conclusions. The IPM book is written in the same style as our earlier BPA book (and the AHM books) and we use JAGS as our (Bayesian) model fitting engine. There will also be an R package called 'IPMbook', for which we are again deeply indebted to Mike Meredith.

We would be very happy if some people could volunteer to check a chapter or two for errors, both in the text and also by running all the code and seeing whether it works. messages.subject: Re: MultiBUGS benchmarks on different computers
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I'm not sure if anyone else has been using MultiBUGS since this message, but I'm getting the same trap errors as Mathias. I'd love to be able to use MultiBUGS as it'll be faster than OpenBUGS or JAGS, but for now it's impossible.

On Tuesday, October 8, 2019 at 9:17:46 AM UTC+11 mato...@gmail.com wrote:
>
> Hi Nathan,
>
> thanks for that summary. This made me look at MultiBUGS again. I had looked at it a while back and ran into a range of issues. After spending another day with it I still have the same issues. While simple occupancy models run fine, I keep getting a range of trap errors with more complex occupancy and SCR models, all of which run fine in JAGS. Errors change depending on the initial values provided but none of the errors point to a specific issue. The most persistent one is Trap 101   (invariant violated). Models compile fine and initialize but throw an error after the MPImsimp initiation. No idea what is going wrong.
>
> If you (or anyone else) has any advice on how to avoid some of these issues that would be great. I have several projects where I could really use MulitBUGS to reduce run times and I have the hardware to take advantage of it.
>
> Thanks,
>
> Mathias
>
>
>
>
> On 28.09.2019 02:00, Kery Marc wrote:
> > Thanks for the interesting report, Nathan.
> >
> > Makes me think about buying some new stuff...
> >
> > Regards  --- Marc
> > From: hmec...@googlegroups.com [hmec...@googlegroups.com] on behalf of Nathan B [twa...@gmail.com]
> > Sent: 27 September 2019 21:23
> > To: hmecology: Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology
> > Subject: MultiBUGS benchmarks on different computers
> >
> > I have recently been using MultiBUGS to run some closed-population modeling code from the Kery and Schaub book that I've modified to work across multiple occasions. Just to give you a feel for the size of the dataset, there are 15 occasions with a total of 13,832 individuals (including the augmented "fake" ones). I also estimate the effect of size class (3 categories) on detection. I was wondering which computer I had available to me would give me the fastest run times.
> >
> > I recorded the run time for the first 1000 samples on three different machines using MultiBUGS. For each machine, I distributed MultiBUGS to run on all possible threads. So for example, my work desktop is a 4 core machine with Hyperthreading = 8 threads. The machines represent different ages of CPU technology and a variety of thread counts. My work desktop is a relatively new machine (about a year old). The server I had access to was around five years old or so, and is pretty slow on single-threaded basis (around 3.5 Ghz boost), but has 40 available threads. Finally I compared these to a new Ryzen 3900x computer that runs 24 threads, but at a slightly lower freq that the Intel (about 4.1 GHz).
> >
> > 1) Intel desktop- Intel Xeon W-2125 (4 cores/8 threads; 4.4Ghz boost).                Run time: 122s.  CPU usage: 99%
> > 2) Server- Intel E5-2687Wv3 x2 (10C/20T x 2 CPUs=40 threads; 3.5Ghz boost). Run time 84s.     CPU usage 75%
> > 3) Ryzen desktop- AMD Ryzen 3900x (12C/24T ~ 4.1GHz boost).                        Run time 50s.     CPU usage 91%
> >
> > As you can see, running MultiBUGS on a machine with lots of threads substantially improves the run time, and it pays to have newer tech...big surprise there :) . The 5-year old 40 core machine (~$10k) was well outpaced by a consumer desktop (~$1k). Also note that CPU usage varies. I've noticed this between models as well. I have a growth model that does not seem to take advantage of the full CPU power when distributed across multiple cores, no matter which computer I used, but was still faster than running single-threaded. Here are those results:
> >
> >     Xeon Server (2x 10/20T): 105s. CPU usage 28%
> >     Xeon desktop (W-2125 4/8T): 85s CPU usage 47%
> >     Ryzen desktop (3900x 12/24T): 40s CPU usage 31%
> >
> > In this case, with the lower CPU usage, the Xeon desktop now outpaces the Server, presumably because the thread count matters less and the cpu speed comes into play more. But the Ryzen chip with fewer threads than the server and lower clock than the Intel desktop still blows both of them out of the water.
> >
> > I really look forward to the development of MultiBUGS and newer, faster, cheaper multi-core processors.
> >
> > Nathan

messages.subject: FW: Vacancy for senior statistician at the IATTC
messages.subject_clean: Vacancy for senior statistician at the IATTC
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

two interesting job announcement.

Best regards  --- Marc

https://www.iattc.org/StaffVacancies/_English/IATTC-Senior%20Statistician.pdf

This is a permanent position as a senior statistician, so a good background in both theoretical and applied statistics and related experience is essential for the position. A few medium term projects that the person would work on include

1.       Spatial temporal modelling of skipjack tuna tagging data to deal with spatially limited tagging and the consequent initial non-mixing. This would involve joining a spatio-temporal model of the population distribution with an advection-diffusion model of the tagged individuals. https://www.iattc.org/Meetings/Meetings2021/SAC-12/Docs/_English/SAC-12-06_%20Assessment%20methods%20for%20skipjack%20in%20the%20EPO%20using%20tagging%20data.pdf

2.       Close-kin mark-recapture. This involves using genetics to “tag” adults through kinship (parent offspring pairs and half sibling pairs) and requires developing statistics for the probability of these events and integrating it with the stock assessment model. Experience with statistical analysis of genetic data would be beneficial.  https://www.iattc.org/Meetings/Meetings2021/SAC-12/Docs/_English/SAC-12-14_Considerations%20for%20conducting%20Close%20Kin%20Mark%20Recapture%20of%20stocks%20managed%20by%20IATTC.pdf

3.       Sampling design. The IATTC has substantial observer and port sampling programs, and assists and advises member countries on their sampling programs. The statistical would work on improving, setting up, and analyzing data from several sampling programs.  Experience with sampling programs would be useful.

Our work is also associated with the Center for the Advancement of Population Assessment Methodology (CAPAM)  http://www.capamresearch.org/
